timecoded_text_to_speech.text: A film in three minutes. Run, low the run.
OK, so your boyfriend has just called you an
affrantic blaze of desperation and needs 100,000
Deutschmarks in 20 minutes, otherwise he'll be dead.
And go. Got any ideas?
Will you better? Because from this moment on,
the clock is ticking. And in 1998, that's exactly what happens in
Tom Tiker's fast-paced experimental thriller, Run, Low the Run.
Set in Berlin, the story follows Lola, played by Frank
a Patenta, who must help her boyfriend Mani, played by
Moritz Bliptoi, raised 100,000 Deutschmarks in order to pay
off alone to her criminal gangster. In her frantic rush to find
Mani and figure out a way to save his life, the pair eventually
rob a supermarket before being chased down by the police.
In her frantic rush to find Mani and figure out a way to save his life,
Lola forces her father at gunpoint to help her rob the banky
works at before taking the money and trying to reach Mani in time.
In her frantic rush to find Mani and figure out a way to save his
life, Lola tries to win the 100,000 needed at a nearby casino,
betting everything she has on her before the clock reaches midday.
For those unfamiliar with the unique narrative format in Tiker's film,
Run, Low the Run, or Lola Rent in German, acts as a collection of free shorter stories,
all of which encompass Lola's desperate quest to help Mani get the money he needs
before the clock strikes 12. Each of the three alternate narratives have their own subtle
differences and consequences for Lola, but all three are connected by repeating
characters and motifs, an ambulance driver not paying attention to the road,
a lover's argument between Lola's father and his mistress,
or the cyclist attempting to sell Lola his bike. All of these supporting elements
are interconnected and play on the idea of how a small difference in timing
can have dramatic ripple effects for others elsewhere.
But this experimental approach to constructing the story would perhaps have had far less impact,
if not for Tiker's stylish direction and cinematographer Frank Greiber's wholly original
visual approach. Combining various film formats with animation, flash photography and split-screen
montages, that give the film its high octane kinetic energy. Energy 2 is personified in
Frank's performance as the frenzy Lola, with her determination to save Mani becoming
increasingly relentless as each of the stories play out. The many shots of her zooming past the
streets of central Berlin are repeated time and time again, providing some nail-biting close calls
as Lola fights against the clock. The end result, combined with music written by the director himself,
gives the film a rollercoaster pace, making us as the viewer feel as exhausted from Lola's running
as she is herself. It's ending or rather it's three different endings vary in their levels of
impact for the viewer, but the visual thrill ride each takes us on acts as the most lasting
element of the film's running time, pardon the pun. In the director's own words, a movie about
life that doesn't confront us with drastic imagery doesn't represent life. In the case of
Run Lola Run, true words have never been spoken.

youtube_description:
#afilminthreeminutes #runlolarun #tomtykwer

Get your shoes on and prepare for the run of your life in Tom Tykwer's experimental thriller "Run Lola Run" or "Lola rennt" in German, a visually unique chase movie that combines multiple film formats with an electrifying techno score. Starring Franka Potente, Mortiz Bleibtreu and Herbert Knaup. Cinematography by Frank Griebe, music by Tom Tykwer, Johnny Kilmek and Reinhold Heil.
